client: I've been really struggling since my grandma passed away last month. Every time I try to work, I just keep remembering little things about her and then I can't concentrate. I don't know if talking about it will help - the sadness just feels so heavy and permanent.
therapist: I hear how deeply this loss is affecting you, and it makes complete sense that these memories feel so heavy right now. When those thoughts about your grandma come up at work, do you notice any particular patterns in what triggers them or how your mind responds?

client:
It's usually the small things that trigger the memories, like when I'm organizing files at work and come across her handwriting on old documents. My mind immediately jumps to how I should have visited her more often before she passed. I know it's irrational, but the guilt just floods in and makes it hard to focus on anything else. 

Sometimes I wonder if talking about these triggers will actually help, or if it'll just make me dwell on them more. The thoughts already feel so overwhelming when they come up.
therapist: It sounds like these moments bring up both deep sadness and painful self-judgment about what you "should" have done differently. When those guilty thoughts arise, have you noticed any evidence that might challenge the idea that you didn't visit enough?

client: I know logically that I visited as much as I could given my work schedule at the time, but that doesn't stop me from feeling like it wasn't enough. The guilt comes from knowing I could have made more effort - skipped a few work days, stayed up later to visit after shifts - but I didn't.
therapist: I hear how this guilt feels so convincing even when you know the facts of your situation. That tension between what we know logically and what we feel emotionally can be especially painful with grief. What do you think your grandma would say about how you're judging yourself right now?

client:
I don't know... I think my grandma would probably tell me not to be so hard on myself. But that's the problem - I can imagine her saying that, but it doesn't make the guilt go away. It's like my brain knows one thing but my heart keeps punishing me anyway. 

The worst part is that I keep replaying all the times I could have visited her more often before she passed. Logically I know I did my best, but it never feels like enough when I think about it at night.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between this loving wisdom from your grandma and the painful self-criticism that keeps resurfacing, especially at night when things feel quiet. Would it help if we explored what "doing your best" actually looked like during that time—the real constraints you were facing?

client: I guess I've never really thought about what "doing my best" actually meant back then. Part of me feels like if I had just tried harder, pushed through the exhaustion, maybe things would've turned out differently. But another part remembers how drained I was, working two jobs while taking care of her. It's confusing because both feelings feel true at the same time.
therapist: This ambivalence sounds so difficult—holding both the compassion for how stretched thin you were and the painful wish that things could have been different. When those conflicting feelings come up, have you noticed if one tends to feel more true in certain moments than others?

client: I think the guilt feels heavier when I'm alone at night. During the day I can rationalize that I was doing my best, but in those quiet moments the "what ifs" just take over. It's like my brain won't let me have both perspectives at once - either I'm the victim of circumstances or I'm the one who failed everyone.
therapist: It makes sense that the quiet nighttime hours make space for this painful either/or thinking to take hold. I'm noticing that even as you describe this pattern, you're showing important awareness of how your perspective shifts—that's actually a really helpful observation for us to work with. What do you think happens in those daytime moments that lets the more compassionate view come through?

client: I guess during the day I'm distracted by work and routines, so there's less room for those harsh thoughts to take over. But sometimes I wonder if the daytime perspective is just me avoiding the truth—like maybe the nighttime thoughts are more honest about how alone I really am. It's hard to trust either version of my thoughts completely.
therapist: It sounds like you're questioning whether you can trust either perspective right now—the daytime distraction or the nighttime self-criticism—and that uncertainty itself feels lonely. When neither version of your thoughts feels completely true, what would it feel like to gently hold space for both, without needing to decide which one is "right"?

client:
That actually makes sense, but it also makes me nervous. If I don't figure out which version is "right," won't I just keep going in circles? At night I'm so sure I messed everything up, but then in the daylight it seems silly. Holding space for both just feels like staying stuck in this back-and-forth forever. 

I guess part of me wants someone to just tell me which thoughts are real, you know? Because when I try to decide for myself, I never trust my own judgment.
therapist: I hear how exhausting this oscillation between perspectives feels, and that understandable desire for someone to just give you the "right" answer about your thoughts. This uncertainty makes me wonder—what would it feel like if, instead of trying to determine which thoughts are "real," we focused on which thoughts are most helpful to you in this grieving process?

client:
I don't know if I can just choose which thoughts are helpful—it feels like I'm lying to myself if I ignore the painful ones. The "unhelpful" thoughts are the ones that feel most true right now, like how I should have done more before they were gone. 

But I'm also so tired of feeling this way all the time. Part of me wants to try what you're saying, but another part is scared that if I stop holding onto the guilt, it means I didn't love them enough.
therapist: I hear how strongly this guilt feels tied to your love for them—like letting go of the pain might mean letting go of how much they mattered to you. That's such a common and understandable fear in grief. Could we explore together what other ways your love for them might show up, beyond just this feeling of guilt?

client: That makes me pause. I don't know...the guilt feels like proof I cared enough, you know? If I stop feeling bad about not being there when they needed me, doesn't that mean I'm moving on too fast? Other ways to show love...I can't really picture that right now. It all just feels empty.
therapist: It sounds like this guilt has become an important emotional connection to your loved one, and the idea of loosening that grip brings up real fears about what might remain. When you think about other ways people honor those they've lost—not to replace your feelings, but to exist alongside them—what small gestures or memories come to mind that might feel meaningful to you?
